### 4.2 Algorithm for Problem 4

Suppose we are given an instance $(A,B,C)$ of Problem 4 with $M=\Theta(n^{d})$ for some constant $0\leq d\leq\mu$ . Define

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}=\left\lfloor\frac{A_{i,k}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{B_{k,j}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{C_{i,j}}{M}\right\rfloor. $$

We also define

$$ A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}=A_{i,k}\bmod M,\qquad B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}=B_{k,j}\bmod M,\qquad C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}=C_{i,j}\bmod M. $$

The high-level outline of our algorithm is as follows:

- 1. Find a “good” modulus $Q$ with $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ . The definition of “good” is deferred to Definition 4.12.

- 2. For every $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , compute $s_{i,j}$ , the number of $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ .

- 3. For every $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , compute $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ , the number of $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ .

- 4. For each $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , output Yes if and only if $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ .

We will prove that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ if and only if $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . Hence, there exists a witness $k$ if and only if $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ . We first prove two simple facts that bound $\lvert A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}\rvert$ , depending on whether $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ , and then prove the correctness of the algorithm assuming that our subroutines are correct.

#### Fact 4.5.

For every $(i,k,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]\times[n^{c}]$ , if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ , then $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}|\geq 7M/10$ .

#### Proof.

We decompose $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}=M\cdot\bigl(A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}\bigr)+\bigl(A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}\bigr)$ . If $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}\neq 0$ , then $|A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}|\geq 1$ . By the promise of Problem 4, $|A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}|\leq|A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}|+|B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}|+|C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}|\leq 3M/10$ . Therefore, using $|a+b|\geq|a|-|b|$ , we have

$$ \bigl|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}\bigr|\geq M\cdot\bigl|A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}\bigr|-\bigl|A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}\bigr|\geq M-3M/10=7M/10. $$

∎

#### Fact 4.6.

For every $(i,k,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]\times[n^{c}]$ , if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ , then $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}|\leq 3M/10$ .

#### Proof.

Since $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=0$ , we have $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}|=|A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}|\leq 3M/10$ by the same argument as in Fact 4.5. ∎

Recall that $s_{i,j}$ is the number of $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ , and $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ is the number of $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . We now prove the correctness of our algorithm.

#### Lemma 4.7 (Correctness).

For every $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , there exists $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ if and only if $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $(i,j)$ and suppose there exists $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ . Then $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ , so this $k$ contributes one to $s_{i,j}$ . Moreover, under the promise of Problem 4, we have $A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}\leq 2M/10$ , so adding the low parts creates no carry across a multiple of $M$ . Hence, $C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=\lfloor C_{i,j}/M\rfloor=\lfloor(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j})/M\rfloor=A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}$ . Therefore, this $k$ does not contribute to $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ , and so $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ .

Conversely, suppose $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ . Then there exists $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . By Fact 4.6, we have $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}|\leq 3M/10<Q$ . Since $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}$ is a multiple of $Q$ and has magnitude strictly less than $Q$ , it must be zero. Therefore, $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ . ∎

In the following sections, we describe how to compute $s_{i,j}$ and $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ efficiently, and how to choose and find a modulus $Q$ . To this end, we introduce several objects used by the subroutines and their analysis. We first provide some intuition. As in [11], we view each pair of row-monotone rows $B_{k,*}$ and $C_{i,*}$ through a level- $\ell$ “coarse lens,” by rounding entries down to multiples of $2^{\ell}$ . This partitions the column indices into contiguous blocks on which both rounded rows are constant; these blocks are called level- $\ell$ segments. Within a segment, the values $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ vary by at most $2^{\ell}$ , so checking a modular relation at the segment start (namely, $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}$ , where $j_{0}$ is the segment start) represents the entire segment up to an additive slack of $\pm 4\cdot 2^{\ell}$ . We call a segment active (with respect to a modulus $Q$ ) if the corresponding modular relation can hold for some shift in $[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ while the high parts indicate that equality does not hold. Thus, active segments capture the remaining “spurious” modular matches. Finally, a modulus $Q$ is good if, for every level $\ell$ , it leaves only a few active segments so that we can afford to enumerate and eliminate all spurious matches.

More formally, let ${\ell_{\max}}$ be such that $M/20\leq 2^{{\ell_{\max}}}<M/10$ .

#### Definition 4.8 (Segments).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , a level- $\ell$ segment is a triple $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ such that for every $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , $\lfloor B_{k,j_{0}}/2^{\ell}\rfloor=\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ and $\lfloor C_{i,j_{0}}/2^{\ell}\rfloor=\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ , and $[j_{0},j_{1}]$ cannot be extended further.

#### Fact 4.9.

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , the total number of level- $\ell$ segments is $\mathcal{O}(n^{a+b+\mu}/2^{\ell})$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ . For each $j\in[n^{c}]$ , define $b_{j}:=\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ and $c_{j}:=\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ . Both sequences $(b_{j})_{j}$ and $(c_{j})_{j}$ are monotone. Since all entries of $B$ and $C$ are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ , each of $(b_{j})_{j}$ and $(c_{j})_{j}$ is bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu}/2^{\ell})$ , and therefore each has at most $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu}/2^{\ell})$ constant blocks. A level- $\ell$ segment is a maximal interval on which both sequences are constant; thus the number of level- $\ell$ segments is $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu}/2^{\ell})$ . Summing over all $n^{a}n^{b}$ choices of $(i,k)$ gives $\mathcal{O}(n^{a+b+\mu}/2^{\ell})$ segments in total. ∎

#### Definition 4.10 (Active segment).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , a level- $\ell$ segment $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is called active with respect to $Q$ if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}}$ and there exists $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q}$ .

#### Definition 4.11 (Set of active segments).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , let $S_{\ell}(Q)$ be the set of all level- $\ell$ segments that are active with respect to $Q$ .

#### Definition 4.12 (Good modulus).

We say that an integer $Q$ is a good modulus if $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ and $|S_{\ell}(Q)|\leq\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ for all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ .

### 4.3 Computing $s_{i,j}$ and $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$

Recall that $s_{i,j}$ is the number of indices $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ . We compute $s_{i,j}$ for all $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ using polynomial matrix multiplication, which reduces modular counting to ordinary rectangular matrix multiplication.

#### Lemma 4.13 (Computing $s_{i,j}$ ).

We can compute $s_{i,j}$ for every $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Qn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time.

#### Proof.

Work over the ring $R:=\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{Q}-1)$ , where $\mathbb{F}$ has characteristic larger than $n^{b}$ . Define an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix $A^{\prime}$ and an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix $B^{\prime}$ over $R$ by

$$ A^{\prime}_{i,k}(x):=x^{A_{i,k}\bmod Q},\qquad B^{\prime}_{k,j}(x):=x^{B_{k,j}\bmod Q}. $$

Compute the matrix product $P(x):=A^{\prime}(x)\cdot B^{\prime}(x)$ over $R$ using fast rectangular matrix multiplication. For each residue $r\in\{0,1,\ldots,Q-1\}$ , the coefficient of $x^{r}$ in $P_{i,j}(x)$ is the number of indices $k\in[n^{b}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv r\pmod{Q}$ . Hence, we set $s_{i,j}$ to be the coefficient of $x^{C_{i,j}\bmod Q}$ in $P_{i,j}(x)$ . Since multiplication in $R$ reduces exponents modulo $Q$ , multiplying two entries costs $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Q)$ field operations, and the overall matrix multiplication takes $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Qn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time. ∎

Recall that $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ is the number of indices $k$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . Suppose that $Q$ is a good modulus as defined in Definition 4.12; we show how to find such a modulus in the next section. For simplicity, let $S_{\ell}$ denote the set of all active level- $\ell$ segments, suppressing the dependence on $Q$ . At a high level, we compute $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ for all $(i,j)$ using $S_{0}$ . Indeed, since $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ are constant on a level- $0$ segment, the congruence $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ can be tested at a single $j$ and then applied to the entire interval $[j_{0},j_{1}]$ in a segment. To compute $S_{0}$ , we compute the sets $S_{\ell}$ via a top-down refinement from level ${\ell_{\max}}$ to level $0$ . To formalize our idea, we prove a property on which our algorithm relies.

#### Lemma 4.14.

For all $0\leq\ell<{\ell_{\max}}$ , and $(i,k,[j_{0}^{\prime},j_{1}^{\prime}])\in S_{\ell}$ , the unique level- $(\ell+1)$ segment $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ with $[j_{0}^{\prime},j_{1}^{\prime}]\subseteq[j_{0},j_{1}]$ is active, i.e., $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])\in S_{\ell+1}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . By definition of a level- $(\ell+1)$ segment, we have $\lfloor B_{k,j_{0}}/2^{\ell+1}\rfloor=\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell+1}\rfloor$ . Hence, $|B_{k,j}-B_{k,j_{0}}|<2^{\ell+1}<M/10$ . Moreover, $|B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j_{0}}|\leq M/10$ by the promise of Problem 4. Hence, if $B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}$ , then

$$ |B_{k,j}-B_{k,j_{0}}|=|(B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}-B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}})M+(B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j_{0}})|\geq M-|B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}-B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j_{0}}|\geq 9M/10, $$

which contradicts the previous bound. Therefore, $B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}$ is constant for $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , and by a similar argument, $C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ is constant for $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Now, since $(i,k,[j_{0}^{\prime},j_{1}^{\prime}])\in S_{\ell}$ , we have $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}}\neq 0$ . Because $j_{0}^{\prime}\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , we conclude that $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}}\neq 0$ , satisfying the high-part condition of being active.

For the congruence condition, note that $[j_{0}^{\prime},j_{1}^{\prime}]\subseteq[j_{0},j_{1}]$ and $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $(\ell+1)$ segment. Hence, $|B_{k,j_{0}}-B_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}|<2^{\ell+1}$ and $|C_{i,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}}|<2^{\ell+1}$ , which implies

$$ |(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}})-(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}})|<2\cdot 2^{\ell+1}. $$

Since $(i,k,[j_{0}^{\prime},j_{1}^{\prime}])\in S_{\ell}$ , we have $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}}\equiv s^{\prime}\pmod{Q}$ for some $s^{\prime}\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ . Take

$$ s=s^{\prime}+(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}})-(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}}). $$

Then $|s|<4\cdot 2^{\ell}+2\cdot 2^{\ell+1}=4\cdot 2^{\ell+1}$ and

$$ (A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}})\equiv s-s^{\prime}+(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{i,j_{0}^{\prime}})\equiv s\pmod{Q}. $$

Thus, the level- $(\ell+1)$ segment $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is active. ∎

#### Lemma 4.15 (Computing $S_{0}$ ).

We can compute $S_{0}$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ time.

#### Proof.

We first compute all level- ${\ell_{\max}}$ segments as follows. For each $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , we use binary search on $j$ to group maximal consecutive indices on which $\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}}\rfloor$ and $\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}}\rfloor$ are both constant. We then enumerate all those level- ${\ell_{\max}}$ segments and filter the active ones to obtain $S_{{\ell_{\max}}}$ . Next, for $\ell={\ell_{\max}}-1,\ldots,0$ , we construct $S_{\ell}$ from $S_{\ell+1}$ as follows. Every segment in $S_{\ell+1}$ refines into $\mathcal{O}(1)$ level- $\ell$ subsegments, since decreasing $\ell$ by $1$ can split a maximal constant block into at most two blocks for $B$ and at most two blocks for $C$ . We use binary search to compute these subsegments. For each resulting subsegment, we test whether it is active at level $\ell$ and, if so, insert it into $S_{\ell}$ .

For correctness, note that every active level- $\ell$ segment is a subsegment of an active level- $(\ell+1)$ segment by Lemma 4.14, and so the correctness follows inductively.

By Fact 4.9, there are $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}})$ level- ${\ell_{\max}}$ segments. Thus, computing them via binary search and constructing $S_{{\ell_{\max}}}$ takes $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}})=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/M)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ time. For the refinement, we note that $Q$ is a good modulus, so for each $\ell$ , we have $|S_{\ell}|=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ , and each active segment generates only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ subsegments. There are $\mathcal{O}(\log M)=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$ levels, so the total time spent in this refinement step is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.16 (Computing $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ ).

We can compute $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ for all $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q+n^{a+c})$ .

#### Proof.

We first compute the set $S_{0}$ using Lemma 4.15. To compute all $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ , we aggregate the contributions of active level- $0$ segments in $S_{0}$ as follows. For each fixed $i\in[n^{a}]$ , we maintain a difference array $D_{i}$ of length $n^{c}+1$ , indexed by $1,\ldots,n^{c}+1$ , and initialized to zero. For each active level- $0$ segment $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])\in S_{0}$ , we test whether $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}$ . If the test succeeds, we increment $D_{i}[j_{0}]$ by one and decrement $D_{i}[j_{1}+1]$ by one. After processing all active level- $0$ segments, we compute prefix sums and set

$$ s^{\prime}_{i,j}=\sum_{1\leq t\leq j}D_{i}[t]\qquad\text{for all }j=1,\ldots,n^{c}. $$

For correctness, fix any triple $(i,k,j)$ counted in $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ . Then we have $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . Let $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ be the unique level- $0$ segment such that $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Since $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $0$ segment, the values $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ are constant over all $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Since $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , we have

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}=A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}} $$

and

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}. $$

Hence, $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is an active level- $0$ segment in $S_{0}$ , and the algorithm performs the range update for $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ . We claim that this update increases the reconstructed value $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ by one (for this $k$ ) exactly when $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Indeed, for any $j\in[n^{c}]$ ,

- • If $j<j_{0}$ , the prefix sum does not include the increment at position $j_{0}$ , so $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ stays the same.

- • If $j_{0}\leq j\leq j_{1}$ , the prefix sum includes the increment at $j_{0}$ but not the decrement at $j_{1}+1$ , so $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ increases by one.

- • If $j\geq j_{1}+1$ , the prefix sum includes both the increment at $j_{0}$ and the decrement at $j_{1}+1$ , which cancel, so $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ stays the same.

Conversely, whenever the algorithm performs a range update for $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])\in S_{0}$ , we have $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}$ . Since $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $0$ segment, the values $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ are constant over all $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Therefore, $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ for every $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Moreover, the segment is active, so $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ for every $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , and the update contributes exactly the intended triples to $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ .

For the running time, scanning all segments in $S_{0}$ and performing the constant-time test and update takes $\mathcal{O}(|S_{0}|)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ . The total time to compute prefix sums is $\mathcal{O}(n^{a+c})$ , since for each fixed $i$ we scan $j=1,\ldots,n^{c}$ once. Together with the time to compute $S_{0}$ , which is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ by Lemma 4.15, this yields the claimed running time. ∎

### 4.4 Finding a Good Modulus $Q$

We now construct a good modulus $Q$ , namely an integer $Q$ with $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ such that the number of active level- $\ell$ segments is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)$ for every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ .

Let $4\leq R\leq n^{o(1)}$ be a parameter to be fixed later, and let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of primes in $[R/2,R]$ . We take $Q$ to be a product of primes $p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{T}$ with $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ for all $1\leq t\leq T$ . Intuitively, each new prime factor filters out many spurious congruences, so the number of active segments shrinks rapidly with $t$ . We choose these primes inductively: at step $t\geq 1$ , we select a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ and multiply it into the current modulus $Q_{t-1}$ , obtaining

$$ Q_{t}:=\prod_{i=1}^{t}p_{i},\qquad\text{where }Q_{0}:=1. $$

For the analysis, define $X_{\ell,t}$ as the number of pairs $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ , where $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ , such that

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t}}\quad\text{and}\quad A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\neq s. $$

Our inductive invariant for $Q_{t}$ is that

$$ X_{\ell,t}=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Later, we choose $R$ so that $X_{\ell,T}=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q_{T})$ . Then, by the following lemma, $Q_{T}$ is a good modulus.

#### Lemma 4.17.

For every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , we have $|S_{\ell}(Q_{T})|\leq X_{\ell,T}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])\in S_{\ell}(Q_{T})$ . By definition of an active segment, there exists an integer $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{T}}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}}$ . We claim that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\neq s$ . Indeed, since $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}}$ , Fact 4.5 implies $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}|\geq 7M/10$ . On the other hand, $|s|\leq 4\cdot 2^{\ell}\leq 4\cdot 2^{{\ell_{\max}}}<4M/10<7M/10$ , so $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\neq s$ . Therefore, every active segment in $S_{\ell}(Q_{T})$ yields a pair $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ counted by $X_{\ell,T}$ , and hence $|S_{\ell}(Q_{T})|\leq X_{\ell,T}$ . ∎

We now explain how to choose $p_{t}$ so that the invariant Eq. 3 continues to hold. For the base case $t=0$ , we set $Q_{0}:=1$ . Since $X_{\ell,0}$ counts level- $\ell$ segment–shift pairs, we trivially have $X_{\ell,0}\leq n^{a+b+\mu}$ by Fact 4.9, and thus $Q_{0}$ satisfies the invariant. Now assume Eq. 3 holds for $t-1$ and that $Q_{t-1}$ is fixed. For any prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , let $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ denote the value of $X_{\ell,t}$ when $Q_{t}$ is set to $Q_{t-1}\cdot p$ . Our goal is to find a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that Eq. 3 holds with respect to $X_{\ell,t}(p_{t})$ .

Such a prime exists; applying the following lemma inductively yields the entire sequence $p_{1},\ldots,p_{T}$ .

#### Lemma 4.18.

There exists $p^{*}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p^{*})=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Moreover, for every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , if $p$ is chosen uniformly at random from $\mathcal{P}$ , then

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\bigl[X_{\ell,t}(p)\bigr]=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right). $$

#### Proof.

Fix a level $\ell$ . Let $\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}$ be the set of all pairs $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ counted by $X_{\ell,t-1}$ ; that is, all pairs satisfying

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t-1}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\neq s, $$

where $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ . For a prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , such a pair is counted in $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ if and only if, additionally, $p$ divides $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}-s$ . Therefore,

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p)=\sum_{((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[p\mid\bigl(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}-s\bigr)\right]. $$

Now choose $p$ uniformly at random from $\mathcal{P}$ . Fix any $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}$ and define

$$ \Delta:=A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}-s. $$

Note that $\Delta\neq 0$ by the definition of $X_{\ell,t-1}$ . Since the entries of $A,B$ and $C$ are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ and $|s|\leq 4\cdot 2^{\ell}\leq 4\cdot 2^{{\ell_{\max}}}=\mathcal{O}(M)=n^{O(1)}$ , we have $|\Delta|=n^{O(1)}$ and hence $\log|\Delta|=\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ . Any prime divisor of $\Delta$ in $[R/2,R]$ is at least $R/2$ , so the number of such prime divisors is at most

$$ \frac{\log|\Delta|}{\log(R/2)}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{\log(R/2)}\right). $$

By the prime number theorem, $|\mathcal{P}|=\Theta(R/\log R)$ , and thus

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}[p\mid\Delta]=\frac{\mathcal{O}(\log n/\log(R/2))}{|\mathcal{P}|}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\cdot\frac{\log R}{\log(R/2)}\right)=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right), $$

where the last equality uses

$$ \frac{\log R}{\log(R/2)}=\frac{\log R}{\log R-\log 2}\leq 2\qquad\text{for }R\geq 4. $$

Then, by linearity of expectation,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}[X_{\ell,t}(p)] \displaystyle=\sum_{((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\left[p\mid\bigl(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}-s\bigr)\right] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}}\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right) \displaystyle=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right), $$

as desired.

To prove the existence of $p^{*}$ , let $L:={\ell_{\max}}+1$ . Recall that $2^{{\ell_{\max}}}=\Theta(M)$ and $M=n^{O(1)}$ , so $L=O(\log M)=O(\log n)$ . From the expectation bound proved above, there exists an absolute constant $C_{0}>0$ such that for every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ ,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\bigl[X_{\ell,t}(p)\bigr]\leq C_{0}\cdot X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\frac{\log n}{R}. $$

By Markov’s inequality, for any $c>0$ ,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\left[X_{\ell,t}(p)>c\cdot C_{0}\cdot\frac{\log n}{R}\,X_{\ell,t-1}\right]\leq\frac{1}{c}. $$

Set $c:=2L$ and apply a union bound over all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ to get

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\left[\exists\,\ell\in\{0,\ldots,{\ell_{\max}}\}:\ X_{\ell,t}(p)>2LC_{0}\cdot\frac{\log n}{R}\,X_{\ell,t-1}\right]\leq\frac{L}{2L}=\frac{1}{2}<1. $$

Hence, there exists $p^{*}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that for all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ ,

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p^{*})\leq 2LC_{0}\cdot\frac{\log n}{R}\,X_{\ell,t-1}=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot O\!\left(\frac{L\log n}{R}\right)=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot O\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right). $$

∎

We now discuss how to deterministically select these primes. For this, it is convenient to track the following quantities as well.

- 1. Let $Y_{\ell,t}$ denote the number of pairs $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ , where $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ , satisfying

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t}}. $$

- 2. Let $Z_{\ell}$ denote the number of pairs $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ , where $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ , satisfying

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}=s. $$

As with $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ , let $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ denote the value of $Y_{\ell,t}$ when the modulus is $Q_{t-1}\cdot p$ .

The high-level idea for selecting $p_{t}$ is as follows. Fix a level $\ell$ . As briefly mentioned in Section 2, directly minimizing $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ would require naively enumerating all level- $\ell$ segments, which is expensive. The key observation is that

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p)=Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Z_{\ell}, $$

where $Z_{\ell}$ depends only on the instance and $\ell$ and is independent of $p$ . Hence, when comparing primes, this unknown offset cancels. In particular,

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p)-\min_{p^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}X_{\ell,t}(p^{\prime})=Y_{\ell,t}(p)-\min_{p^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}}Y_{\ell,t}(p^{\prime}). $$

Therefore, it suffices to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and choose a prime $p$ such that $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ is close to its minimum simultaneously for all levels. The process of computing $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ will be essentially the same as how we computed $s_{i,j}$ : we reduce modular counting to rectangular matrix multiplication over a polynomial ring. The only difference is that we count segments, identified by boundary indicators, rather than all column indices. More formally, we have the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.19 (Computing $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ ).

We can compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all primes $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all levels $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ .

#### Proof.

Fix a prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and a level $\ell$ . We present an algorithm to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for the modulus $Q^{\prime}=Q_{t-1}\cdot p$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}\,n^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time. Since there are ${\ell_{\max}}=\mathcal{O}(\log M)=\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ levels, $|\mathcal{P}|=\Theta(R/\log R)=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(R)$ , and $Q^{\prime}=Q_{t-1}\cdot p\leq Q_{t-1}R$ , the total running time to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all levels is

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{O}}(|\mathcal{P}|\cdot{\ell_{\max}}\cdot(RQ_{t-1})\,n^{\omega(a,b,c)})=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)}). $$

Recall that $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ counts pairs $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ where $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $\ell$ segment, $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ , and $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ . A level- $\ell$ segment $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a maximal interval on which both $\left\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor$ and $\left\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor$ are constant. Therefore, $[j_{0},j_{1}]$ starts at column $j$ if and only if either $j=1$ , or at least one of $\left\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor$ and $\left\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor$ changes at $j$ . Hence, it suffices to check each segment exactly once via its start column $j_{0}$ . More concretely, define an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ boundary indicator matrix $I^{B}$ by

$$ I^{B}_{k,1}:=1,\qquad I^{B}_{k,j}:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\left\lfloor B_{k,j-1}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\neq\left\lfloor B_{k,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\right]\quad(j\geq 2), $$

and an $n^{a}\times n^{c}$ boundary indicator matrix $I^{C}$ by

$$ I^{C}_{i,1}:=1,\qquad I^{C}_{i,j}:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\left\lfloor C_{i,j-1}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\neq\left\lfloor C_{i,j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\right]\quad(j\geq 2). $$

Then it suffices to count, for each $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , the indices $k\in[n^{b}]$ with $I^{B}_{k,j}=1$ or $I^{C}_{i,j}=1$ , grouped by the residue class of $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ , and then weight each residue class by the number of admissible shifts $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ in that class.

To do this, we use the polynomial matrix multiplication technique. Work over the ring $\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{Q^{\prime}}-1)$ , where $\mathbb{F}$ is a field of sufficiently large characteristic. Construct an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix $A^{\prime}$ and two $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrices $B^{\prime}$ and $B^{\mathrm{bdry}}$ by

$$ A^{\prime}_{i,k}(x):=x^{A_{i,k}\bmod{Q^{\prime}}},\qquad B^{\prime}_{k,j}(x):=x^{B_{k,j}\bmod{Q^{\prime}}},\qquad B^{\mathrm{bdry}}_{k,j}(x):=I^{B}_{k,j}\cdot x^{B_{k,j}\bmod{Q^{\prime}}}. $$

Compute the matrix products $D^{\mathrm{all}}:=A^{\prime}\cdot B^{\prime}$ and $D^{\mathrm{bdry}}:=A^{\prime}\cdot B^{\mathrm{bdry}}$ over $\mathcal{R}$ using fast rectangular matrix multiplication, and finally construct an $n^{a}\times n^{c}$ matrix $D$ defined by

$$ D_{i,j}(x):=\begin{cases}D^{\mathrm{all}}_{i,j}(x),&\text{if }I^{C}_{i,j}=1,\\
D^{\mathrm{bdry}}_{i,j}(x),&\text{if }I^{C}_{i,j}=0.\end{cases} $$

For each $r\in\{0,\ldots,Q^{\prime}-1\}$ and $(i,j)$ , let $U_{i,j}(r)$ be the coefficient of $x^{r}$ in $D_{i,j}(x)$ . Then $U_{i,j}(r)$ is the number of indices $k$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv r\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ and either $I^{B}_{k,j}=1$ or $I^{C}_{i,j}=1$ . Next, define

$$ W(r):=\left|\left\{s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]:\ s\equiv r\pmod{Q^{\prime}}\right\}\right|. $$

Note that the pair $((i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}]),s)$ is counted in $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ exactly when $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}-C_{i,j_{0}}\equiv s\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ . Equivalently, if $r\equiv A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ , then $s\equiv r-C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ . Thus, grouping by $r$ , the contribution of a fixed $(i,j)$ to $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ is

$$ \sum_{r=0}^{Q^{\prime}-1}U_{i,j}(r)\cdot W\!\bigl((r-C_{i,j})\bmod Q^{\prime}\bigr), $$

and therefore

$$ Y_{\ell,t}(p)=\sum_{i\in[n^{a}]}\sum_{j\in[n^{c}]}\sum_{r=0}^{Q^{\prime}-1}U_{i,j}(r)\cdot W\!\bigl((r-C_{i,j})\bmod Q^{\prime}\bigr). $$

For the running time, arithmetic in $\mathcal{R}$ reduces exponents modulo $Q^{\prime}$ , so the cost of the rectangular matrix product is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}\,n^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ , and we compute $\mathcal{O}(1)$ such products. Extracting $U_{i,j}(r)$ for all $(i,j)$ and $r$ costs $\mathcal{O}(Q^{\prime}\,n^{a+c})$ , computing $W(r)$ for all $r$ costs $\mathcal{O}(Q^{\prime})$ , and evaluating the triple sum costs $\mathcal{O}(Q^{\prime}\,n^{a+c})$ . Hence, for fixed $p$ and $\ell$ we can compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}\,n^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time. ∎

#### Lemma 4.20.

We can find a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that $p_{t}$ satisfies Eq. 3; that is

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p_{t})=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Moreover, $p_{t}$ can be found in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\bigr)$ time.

#### Proof.

We run the algorithm in Lemma 4.19 to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all primes $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all levels $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ . For each $\ell$ , define

$$ Y^{*}_{\ell,t}:=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}Y_{\ell,t}(p), $$

and choose $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ that minimizes

$$ \Phi(p):=\max_{0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}}\bigl\{Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\bigr\}. $$

For correctness, we first note that $Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\geq Z_{\ell}$ . Since $X_{\ell,t}(p)=Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Z_{\ell}$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and $X_{\ell,t}(p)\geq 0$ , we have $Y_{\ell,t}(p)\geq Z_{\ell}$ for every $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , and thus $Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\geq Z_{\ell}$ .

Now, let $p^{*}\in\mathcal{P}$ be a prime satisfying Eq. 4, which exists by Lemma 4.18. Then, for every $\ell$ ,

$$ Y_{\ell,t}(p^{*})-Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\leq Y_{\ell,t}(p^{*})-Z_{\ell}=X_{\ell,t}(p^{*})=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}, $$

where the last inequality follows from the inductive hypothesis Eq. 3. Therefore,

$$ \Phi(p^{*})=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}, $$

and by the choice of $p_{t}$ minimizing $\Phi$ , we obtain

$$ Y_{\ell,t}(p_{t})-Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\leq\Phi(p_{t})\leq\Phi(p^{*})\leq n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Next, define

$$ X^{*}_{\ell,t}:=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}X_{\ell,t}(p). $$

By minimality and Lemma 4.18,

$$ X^{*}_{\ell,t}\leq\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\bigl[X_{\ell,t}(p)\bigr]=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right)=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right) $$

Using the inductive hypothesis Eq. 3, we obtain

$$ X^{*}_{\ell,t}=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}, $$

Also, since $X_{\ell,t}(p)=Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Z_{\ell}$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and $Z_{\ell}$ is independent of $p$ , we have

$$ Y^{*}_{\ell,t}-Z_{\ell}=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\bigl\{Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Z_{\ell}\bigr\}=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}X_{\ell,t}(p)=X^{*}_{\ell,t}. $$

Combining the above bounds, for every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ we get

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p_{t})=Y_{\ell,t}(p_{t})-Z_{\ell}=\bigl(Y^{*}_{\ell,t}-Z_{\ell}\bigr)+\bigl(Y_{\ell,t}(p_{t})-Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\bigr)\leq X^{*}_{\ell,t}+\Phi(p_{t})=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}. $$

For the running time, computing $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ via Lemma 4.19 dominates, giving $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\bigr)$ time. The remaining steps (taking minima and selecting $p_{t}$ ) take at most $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{P}|{\ell_{\max}})=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(R\log n)$ additional time, which is lower order. ∎

It remains to set the parameters so that the above procedure yields a good modulus. To this end, we prove the following fact.

#### Fact 4.21.

Let $R=2^{\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}\right)}$ and $T=\mathcal{O}(\log n/\log R)$ . Then $(\log n)^{2T}=n^{o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

We write $(\log n)^{2T}=\exp\!\bigl(2T\log\log n\bigr)$ . Thus, it suffices to show that $\exp(2T\log\log n)=n^{o(1)}$ . Indeed,

$$ \exp\!\bigl(2T\log\log n\bigr)=\exp\!\left(2\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log n}{\log R}\right)\cdot\log\log n\right)=\exp\!\left(\mathcal{O}\!\left(\log n\cdot\frac{\log\log n}{\log R}\right)\right). $$

By our choice of $R$ , we have $\log R=\Theta(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})$ , which implies $\log\log n/\log R=o(1)$ . Therefore,

$$ \exp\!\bigl(2T\log\log n\bigr)=\exp\!\bigl(o(\log n)\bigr)=n^{o(1)}, $$

as claimed. ∎

#### Lemma 4.22 (Computing a good modulus).

We can compute a good modulus $Q$ in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ .

#### Proof.

By applying Lemma 4.20 inductively for $T$ steps, we obtain primes $p_{1},\ldots,p_{T}\in\mathcal{P}$ and a modulus $Q_{T}:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}$ such that Eq. 3 holds. Since $p_{t}\in[R/2,R]$ for all $1\leq t\leq T$ , we have $(R/2)^{T}\leq Q_{T}\leq R^{T}$ . In particular, to ensure $Q_{T}\geq M$ it suffices to take

$$ T=\Theta(\log M/\log R)=\mathcal{O}(\log n/\log R). $$

Moreover, if we take $T$ to be the first index such that $Q_{T}\geq M$ , then $Q_{T-1}<M$ and hence $Q_{T}=Q_{T-1}\cdot p_{T}<M\cdot R$ , so $Q_{T}$ overshoots $M$ by at most a factor of $R$ . We set

$$ R=2^{\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}\right)}. $$

Then $R=n^{o(1)}$ , and therefore $M\leq Q_{T}\leq M\cdot R=M\cdot n^{o(1)}$ . Finally, by Fact 4.21, we have $(\log^{2}n)^{T}=n^{o(1)}$ , and so

$$ (\log^{2}n/R)^{T}=(\log n)^{2T}/R^{T}=n^{o(1)}/R^{T}=n^{o(1)}/Q_{T}. $$

Hence $Q_{T}$ satisfies $M\leq Q_{T}\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ , and

$$ X_{\ell,T}=n^{a+b+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{T}=\frac{n^{a+b+\mu+o(1)}}{Q_{T}}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Therefore, $Q_{T}$ is a good modulus.

For the running time, we apply Lemma 4.20 for $T$ steps. At step $t$ , the cost of computing $p_{t}$ is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\right)$ . Since $Q_{t-1}\leq Q_{T-1}<M$ , the total time is

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}R^{2}Q_{t-1}n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\right)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(TR^{2}M\,n^{\omega(a,b,c)}\right)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}\right), $$

where the last bound uses $TR^{2}=n^{o(1)}$ for our choice of $R$ . ∎

### 4.5 Combining the Results

#### Theorem 4.23.

There is a deterministic $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}+n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ -time algorithm for Problem 4.

#### Proof.

We first compute a good modulus $Q$ via Lemma 4.22 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ . Next, we compute $s_{i,j}$ for all $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ via Lemma 4.13 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Qn^{\omega(a,b,c)})=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ . Finally, we compute $s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ for all $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ via Lemma 4.16 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q+n^{a+c}\right)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{a+b+\mu}/M+n^{a+c}\right)$ . For each $(i,j)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{c}]$ , we output Yes if and only if $s_{i,j}>s^{\prime}_{i,j}$ ; correctness follows from Lemma 4.7. The total running time is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}+n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ as claimed. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Our claimed running time is

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{a+c}+n^{b+c}+n^{(a+b+\mu+\omega(a,b,c))/2}\right). $$

Let $d:=(a+b+\mu-\omega(a,b,c))/2$ . Since $\mu\geq 0$ , we have $d\leq\mu$ : indeed, $d>\mu$ would imply $\mu+\omega(a,b,c)<a+b$ , contradicting the trivial lower bound $\omega(a,b,c)\geq a+b$ . Furthermore, we may assume that $d\geq 0$ : if $d<0$ , then $a+b+\mu<\omega(a,b,c)$ . In this case, Lemma 17 of [19] gives an algorithm running in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{a+c}+n^{b+c}+n^{a+b+\mu}\right)$ , which is dominated by our claimed bound. Hence, we may assume $0\leq d\leq\mu$ .

Now, by Lemmas 4.2 and 4.3, it suffices to solve Problem 4. By Theorem 4.23, there is a deterministic algorithm for Problem 4 that runs in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}+n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ . Take $d$ as the exponent for $M$ ; that is, take $M=\Theta\left(n^{(a+b+\mu-\omega(a,b,c))/2}\right)$ . Then the two terms balance, yielding $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}+n^{a+b+\mu}/M\right)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{(a+b+\mu+\omega(a,b,c))/2}\right)$ , which is dominated by our claimed bound. ∎

## 5 Extension to Column-Monotone Min-Plus Product

In this section, we present a deterministic algorithm for column-monotone Min-Plus product, whose definition we recall below.

#### Problem 5.

Let $A$ be an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ integer matrix. Let $B$ be an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ column-monotone integer matrix with entries in $[n^{\mu}]$ . Given $(A,B)$ as input, compute $A\star B$ .

We start by reducing column-monotone Min-Plus product to the following problem, which is a “rotated” version of Problem 3 (the differences have been highlighted).

#### Problem 3’.

Let $A$ be an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ integer matrix with nonnegative entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Let $B$ be an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ row-monotone integer matrix with nonnegative entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Let $C$ be an $n^{a}\times n^{c}$ row-monotone integer matrix with nonnegative entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Given $(A,B,C)$ as input, for every $\boldsymbol{(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]}$ , decide whether there exists $\boldsymbol{j\in[n^{c}]}$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ .

We will show that the running time for Problem ’ is the same as the running time for Problem 3.

#### Theorem 5.1.

There is a deterministic algorithm for Problem ’ that runs in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+c}+n^{b+c}+n^{(a+b+\mu+\omega(a,b,c))/2})$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2 assuming Theorem 5.1.

Let $(A,B)$ be an instance of Problem 5. Similar to the proof of Lemma 4.2, we may assume that all entries of $A$ are nonnegative integers bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . ### 5.1 Algorithm for Problem ’

Using the same proof as for Lemma 4.3, we can reduce Problem ’ to the following problem.

#### Problem 4’.

Let $(A,B,C)$ be an instance of Problem ’, and let $M$ be a positive integer that is a multiple of $100$ and satisfies $M=\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Additionally, assume that for every $i\in[n^{a}]$ , $k\in[n^{b}]$ , and $j\in[n^{c}]$ , we have

$$ A_{i,k}\bmod M,\;B_{k,j}\bmod M,\;C_{i,j}\bmod M\leq\frac{M}{10}. $$

Given $(A,B,C)$ as input, for every $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , decide whether there exists $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ .

As before, we define

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}=\left\lfloor\frac{A_{i,k}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{B_{k,j}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=\left\lfloor\frac{C_{i,j}}{M}\right\rfloor $$

and

$$ A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}=A_{i,k}\bmod M,\qquad B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}=B_{k,j}\bmod M,\qquad C^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,j}=C_{i,j}\bmod M. $$

Our algorithm proceeds as follows:

- 1. Find a “good” modulus $Q$ with respect to Definition 4.12. By Lemma 4.22, it takes $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time.

- 2. For every $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , compute $r_{i,k}$ , the number of $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ . Using the same method as Lemma 4.13, it takes $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Qn^{\omega(a,c,b)})=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ time.

- 3. For every $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , compute $r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ , the number of $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . To do so, first compute $S_{0}(Q)$ using Lemma 4.15 in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/Q)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ time. Fix any triple $(i,k,j)$ that is counted in $r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ , i.e., satisfying $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . Let $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ be the unique level- $0$ segment such that $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . Since $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is a level- $0$ segment, the values $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ are constant over all $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ . We have $j\in[j_{0},j_{1}]$ , so

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j_{0}}=A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j_{0}} $$

and

$$ A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}. $$

Hence, $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ is an active level- $0$ segment in $S_{0}(Q)$ . Therefore, we can enumerate all segments $(i,k,[j_{0},j_{1}])$ in $S_{0}(Q)$ , check whether $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j_{0}}\equiv C_{i,j_{0}}\pmod{Q}$ , and if so, increment $r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ by $j_{1}-j_{0}+1$ . Since $Q$ is a good modulus, we have $|S_{0}(Q)|=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ , so this step takes $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ time.

- 4. For each $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , output Yes if and only if $r_{i,k}>r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ .

The correctness of the algorithm follows from the following lemma.

#### Lemma 5.2.

For every $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , there exists $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ if and only if $r_{i,k}>r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $(i,k)$ and suppose there exists $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ . Then $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ , so this $j$ contributes one to $r_{i,k}$ . Moreover, under the promise of Problem ’, we have $A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{low}}_{k,j}\leq 2M/10$ , so adding the low parts creates no carry across multiples of $M$ . Hence, $C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}=\lfloor C_{i,j}/M\rfloor=\lfloor(A_{i,k}+B_{k,j})/M\rfloor=A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}$ . Thus, this $j$ does not contribute to $r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ , and therefore $r_{i,k}>r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ .

Conversely, suppose $r_{i,k}>r^{\prime}_{i,k}$ . Then there exists $j\in[n^{c}]$ such that $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\equiv C_{i,j}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,k}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k,j}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{i,j}$ . By Fact 4.6, we have $|A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}|\leq 3M/10<Q$ . Since $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}-C_{i,j}$ is a multiple of $Q$ whose magnitude is strictly less than $Q$ , it must be zero. Hence, $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ . ∎

Now the claimed running time in Theorem 5.1 is

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{a+c}+n^{b+c}+n^{(a+b+\mu+\omega(a,b,c))/2}\right). $$

Let $d:=(a+b+\mu-\omega(a,b,c))/2$ . As discussed in the proof of Theorem 1.1, we have $d\leq\mu$ .

If $d\geq 0$ , our approach runs in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega(a,b,c)}+n^{a+b+\mu}/M)$ . Taking $M=\Theta(n^{(a+b+\mu-\omega(a,b,c))/2})$ balances the two terms and gives a running time of $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(a+b+\mu+\omega(a,b,c))/2})$ , which is dominated by the claimed bound.

If $d<0$ , then $a+b+\mu<\omega(a,b,c)$ . In this case, we use a direct approach. For every row of $B$ and $C$ , compute its maximal constant intervals by scanning the row; that is, we partition each row into maximal contiguous intervals on which the row value is constant. This takes $\mathcal{O}(n^{b+c}+n^{a+c})$ time. Since the entries are bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ and the rows are monotone, each row has $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ such intervals. Then, for each pair $(i,k)\in[n^{a}]\times[n^{b}]$ , scan the two interval decompositions of $B_{k,*}$ and $C_{i,*}$ using two pointers, and consider their common refinement: the maximal intervals obtained by intersecting one constant interval of $B_{k,*}$ with one constant interval of $C_{i,*}$ . On each such refined interval, both $B_{k,j}$ and $C_{i,j}$ are constant, so it suffices to check whether $A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}=C_{i,j}$ for one representative $j$ in the interval. Since the common refinement has $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ intervals, all pairs $(i,k)$ can be processed in $\mathcal{O}(n^{a+b+\mu})$ time. Thus the total running time is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{a+c}+n^{b+c}+n^{a+b+\mu})$ , and since $a+b+\mu<\omega(a,b,c)$ , this running time is dominated by the claimed bound.

## 6 Deterministic Monotone Min-Plus Convolution

In this section, we present a deterministic algorithm for monotone Min-Plus convolution, whose definition we recall below.

#### Problem 6.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two monotone arrays of length $n$ with entries in $[n^{\mu}]$ . Given $(A,B)$ as input, compute $A\diamond B$ .

### 6.1 Reduction to a Verification Problem

As in Section 4, we first reduce Problem 6 to a corresponding verification problem and then to a promised version in which all entries have small residues modulo a parameter $M$ .

#### Problem 7.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two monotone arrays of length $n$ with nonnegative entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Let $C$ be an array of length- $2n-1$ indexed by $2$ to $2n$ with nonnegative entries bounded by $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Given $(A,B,C)$ as input, for every $k\in[2,2n]$ , decide whether there exists $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ .

#### Problem 8.

Let $A$ , $B$ , and $C$ be an instance of Problem 7, and let $M$ be a positive integer that is a multiple of $100$ and at most $\mathcal{O}(n^{\mu})$ . Additionally, assume that

$$ A_{i}\bmod M,B_{i}\bmod M,C_{k}\bmod M\leq\frac{M}{10}\qquad\text{ for }\qquad i\in[n],k\in[2,2n]. $$

Given $(A,B,C)$ as input, for every $k\in[2,2n]$ , decide whether there exists $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ .

#### Lemma 6.1.

If there is a $T(n;n^{\mu},M)$ -time deterministic algorithm for Problem 8 for any choice of $M$ , then there is an $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T(n;n^{\mu},M))$ -time deterministic algorithm for Problem 6.

#### Proof sketch.

The proof is similar to the proofs of Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.3. We briefly describe the constructions.

To reduce Problem 6 to Problem 7, we let $A^{\prime}_{i}:=\lfloor A_{i}/2\rfloor$ and $B^{\prime}_{i}:=\lfloor B_{i}/2\rfloor$ . We compute $C^{\prime}:=A^{\prime}\diamond B^{\prime}$ recursively. Construct three candidate arrays by $C^{(s)}_{k}:=2C^{\prime}_{k}+s$ for all $s\in\{0,1,2\}$ . Note that flooring preserves monotonicity, so $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ are also monotone. Therefore, we run the verifier for Problem 7 on $(A,B,C^{(s)})$ for each $s\in\{0,1,2\}$ . By an argument analogous to Lemma 4.2, correctness follows.

Next, we reduce Problem 7 to Problem 8. Let $W:=M/100$ . We may assume that all entries of $A$ , $B$ , and $C$ are at least $M$ by adding $M$ to the entries of $A$ and $B$ and adding $2M$ to the entries of $C$ . We partition $\{0,1,\ldots,M-1\}$ into intervals $I_{s}$ defined by

$$ I_{s}:=[sW,(s+1)W)\qquad\text{for }s\in\{0,1,\ldots,99\}. $$

For each $s\in\{0,1,\ldots,99\}$ , define arrays $A^{(s)}[1,2,\ldots,n]$ and $B^{(s)}[1,2,\ldots,n]$ by

$$ A^{(s)}_{i}:=\begin{cases}A_{i}-sW,&\text{if }A_{i}\bmod M\in I_{s},\\
\Big\lfloor\dfrac{A_{i}-sW}{M}\Big\rfloor\cdot M+3W,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}, $$

and define $B^{(s)}$ analogously. Additionally, for all $s,t\in\{0,1,\ldots,99\}$ , let

$$ J_{s,t}:=\bigl\{(s+t)W\bmod M,\ ((s+t)W+1)\bmod M,\ \ldots,\ ((s+t)W+(2W-1))\bmod M\bigr\}, $$

and define an array $C^{(s,t)}[2,3,\ldots,2n]$ by

$$ C^{(s,t)}_{k}:=\begin{cases}C_{k}-(s+t)W,&\text{if }C_{k}\bmod M\in J_{s,t},\\
\Big\lfloor\dfrac{C_{k}-(s+t)W}{M}\Big\rfloor\cdot M+7W,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

For all $s,t\in\{0,1,\ldots,99\}$ , run the algorithm for Problem 8 on the instances $(A^{(s)},B^{(t)},C^{(s,t)})$ and output Yes for index $k$ if any instance outputs Yes for $k$ . By an argument analogous to Lemma 4.3, correctness follows.

For the running time, we make $\mathcal{O}(1)$ calls to the $T(n;n^{\mu},M)$ -time verifier for Problem 8 per recursion level. The recursion depth is $\mathcal{O}(\log(n^{\mu}))=\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ , which preserves the $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T(n;n^{\mu},M))$ bound. ∎

### 6.2 Algorithm for Problem 8

We focus on solving Problem 8 efficiently. Suppose we are given an instance $(A,B,C)$ of Problem 8 with $M=\mathcal{O}(n^{d})$ for some constant $0\leq d\leq\mu$ . Define

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}=\left\lfloor\frac{A_{i}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad B^{\mathrm{high}}_{j}=\left\lfloor\frac{B_{j}}{M}\right\rfloor,\qquad C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}=\left\lfloor\frac{C_{k}}{M}\right\rfloor. $$

We also define

$$ A^{\mathrm{low}}_{i}=A_{i}\bmod M,\qquad B^{\mathrm{low}}_{j}=B_{j}\bmod M,\qquad C^{\mathrm{low}}_{k}=C_{k}\bmod M. $$

The high-level outline of our algorithm is as follows:

- 1. Find a “good” modulus $Q$ with $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ . The definition of “good” is deferred to Definition 6.9.

- 2. For every $k\in[2,2n]$ , compute $s_{k}$ , the number of indices $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ .

- 3. For every $k\in[2,2n]$ , compute $s^{\prime}_{k}$ , the number of indices $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ .

- 4. For each $k\in[2,2n]$ , output Yes if and only if $s_{k}>s^{\prime}_{k}$ .

We will show that $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ holds if and only if $s_{k}>s^{\prime}_{k}$ . First, we state two facts without proofs, as they are essentially identical to the proofs of Fact 4.5 and Fact 4.6.

#### Fact 6.2.

For every $k\in[2,2n]$ and $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ , if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ , then $|A_{i}+B_{k-i}-C_{k}|\geq 7M/10$ .

#### Fact 6.3.

For every $k\in[2,2n]$ and $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ , if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ , then $|A_{i}+B_{k-i}-C_{k}|\leq 3M/10$ .

#### Lemma 6.4.

For every $k\in[2,2n]$ , there exists $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ if and only if $s_{k}>s^{\prime}_{k}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose there exists $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ . Then $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ , and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ because adding the low parts creates no carry across a multiple of $M$ . Hence, $i$ contributes to $s_{k}$ but not to $s^{\prime}_{k}$ . Conversely, suppose $s_{k}>s^{\prime}_{k}$ . Then there exists $i\in[n]$ such that $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}=C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ . Then $A_{i}+B_{k-i}-C_{k}$ is a multiple of $Q$ , and $|A_{i}+B_{k-i}-C_{k}|<Q$ by Fact 6.3. This implies $A_{i}+B_{k-i}=C_{k}$ . ∎

Let ${\ell_{\max}}$ be such that $M/20\leq 2^{{\ell_{\max}}}<M/10$ . We define segments, active segments, and good modulus analogously to Section 4.

#### Definition 6.5 (Segments).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , a level- $\ell$ segment is a pair $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ such that $[i_{0},i_{1}]\subseteq[\max\{1,k-n\},\min\{n,k-1\}]$ , for every $i\in[i_{0},i_{1}]$ , $\lfloor A_{i_{0}}/2^{\ell}\rfloor=\lfloor A_{i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ , and $\lfloor B_{k-i_{0}}/2^{\ell}\rfloor=\lfloor B_{k-i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ , and $[i_{0},i_{1}]$ cannot be extended further.

#### Definition 6.6 (Active Segment).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , a level- $\ell$ segment $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is called active with respect to $Q$ if $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i_{0}}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i_{0}}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}\neq 0$ and there exists $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ such that $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q}$ .

#### Fact 6.7.

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , the number of level- $\ell$ segments is $\mathcal{O}(n^{1+\mu}/2^{\ell})$ .

#### Definition 6.8 (Set of Active Segments).

For $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , let $S_{\ell}(Q)$ be the set of all active level- $\ell$ segments with respect to $Q$ .

#### Definition 6.9 (Good Modulus).

We say that an integer $Q$ is a good modulus if $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ and $|S_{\ell}(Q)|\leq\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ for all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ .

### 6.3 Computing $s_{k}$ and $s_{k}^{\prime}$

Recall that $s_{k}$ is the number of indices $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ . We compute $s_{k}$ for all $k\in[2,2n]$ using polynomial multiplication.

#### Lemma 6.10 (Computing $s_{k}$ ).

We can compute $s_{k}$ for every $k\in[2,2n]$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Qn)$ time.

#### Proof.

Work over the ring $\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{Q}-1)$ , where $\mathbb{F}$ has characteristic greater than $n$ . Define two bivariate polynomials in $\mathcal{R}[y]$ by

$$ P_{A}(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x^{A_{i}\bmod Q}y^{i},\qquad P_{B}(x,y):=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x^{B_{j}\bmod Q}y^{j}. $$

Compute the product $P(x,y):=P_{A}(x,y)\cdot P_{B}(x,y)$ in $\mathcal{R}[y]$ .

For correctness, fix $k\in[2,2n]$ and $r\in\{0,1,\ldots,Q-1\}$ . The coefficient of $x^{r}y^{k}$ in $P(x,y)$ equals the number of pairs $(i,j)\in[n]\times[n]$ such that $i+j=k$ and $A_{i}+B_{j}\equiv r\pmod{Q}$ . Equivalently, it equals the number of indices $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ and $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv r\pmod{Q}$ . Hence, for each $k\in[2,2n]$ , we set $s_{k}$ to be the coefficient of $x^{C_{k}\bmod Q}y^{k}$ in $P(x,y)$ .

For the running time, the degrees in $x$ and $y$ of $P_{A}$ and $P_{B}$ are at most $Q-1$ and $n$ . Therefore, using fast polynomial multiplication, we can compute $P$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Qn)$ time. ∎

We now describe how to compute $s^{\prime}_{k}$ . Recall that $s^{\prime}_{k}$ is the number of indices $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ , $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ . Assume that $Q$ is a good modulus, as in Definition 6.9. For simplicity, let $S_{\ell}$ denote the set of all active level- $\ell$ segments, suppressing the dependence on $Q$ . We first prove a property that we will use to compute $s^{\prime}_{k}$ .

#### Lemma 6.11.

For all $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}-1$ , and $([i_{0}^{\prime},i_{1}^{\prime}],k)\in S_{\ell}$ , the unique level- $(\ell+1)$ segment $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ such that $[i_{0}^{\prime},i_{1}^{\prime}]\subseteq[i_{0},i_{1}]$ is active, i.e., $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)\in S_{\ell+1}$ .

#### Proof sketch.

By a similar argument to that of Lemma 4.14, we have $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}$ and $B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}$ are constant on $[i_{0},i_{1}]$ . Since $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i_{0}^{\prime}}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i_{0}^{\prime}}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ and $i_{0}^{\prime}\in[i_{0},i_{1}]$ , we conclude that $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i_{0}}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i_{0}}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ , satisfying the first high-part condition of being active.

For the congruence condition, we note that $[i_{0}^{\prime},i_{1}^{\prime}]\subseteq[i_{0},i_{1}]$ and $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a level- $(\ell+1)$ segment. By a similar argument to that of Lemma 4.14, we have

$$ \bigl|(A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k})-(A_{i_{0}^{\prime}}+B_{k-i_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{k})\bigr|<2\cdot 2^{\ell+1}. $$

Since $([i_{0}^{\prime},i_{1}^{\prime}],k)\in S_{\ell}$ , we have $A_{i_{0}^{\prime}}+B_{k-i_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{k}\equiv s^{\prime}\pmod{Q}$ for some $s^{\prime}\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\ 4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ . Let

$$ s=s^{\prime}+(A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k})-(A_{i_{0}^{\prime}}+B_{k-i_{0}^{\prime}}-C_{k}). $$

Then, $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q}$ and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell+1},4\cdot 2^{\ell+1}]$ . ∎

#### Lemma 6.12 (Computing $s^{\prime}_{k}$ ).

We can compute $s^{\prime}_{k}$ for all $k\in[2,2n]$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{1+\mu}/Q\right)$ time.

#### Proof.

As in Lemma 4.16, we first compute $S_{0}$ and then compute the values $s^{\prime}_{k}$ using $S_{0}$ .

- 1. Phase 1: Computing $S_{0}$ . We compute all level- ${\ell_{\max}}$ segments via binary search and keep only the active ones to obtain $S_{{\ell_{\max}}}$ . Next, for $\ell={\ell_{\max}}-1,\ldots,0$ , we construct $S_{\ell}$ from $S_{\ell+1}$ as follows. Each segment in $S_{\ell+1}$ refines into $\mathcal{O}(1)$ level- $\ell$ subsegments, since decreasing $\ell$ by $1$ can split a maximal constant block into at most two blocks for $A$ and at most two blocks for $B$ . We use binary search to find the boundary indices and compute these subsegments. For each resulting subsegment, we test whether it is active, and, if so, insert it into $S_{\ell}$ .

- 2. Phase 2: Computing $s^{\prime}_{k}$ . For each segment $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)\in S_{0}$ , we test whether $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ . If the test succeeds, we increment $s^{\prime}_{k}$ by $i_{1}-i_{0}+1$ .

The correctness of Phase 1 follows inductively using Lemma 6.11. For Phase 2, fix any $i\in[n]$ such that $k-i\in[n]$ , $A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}$ , and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}$ . Let $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ be the unique level- $0$ segment containing $(i,k)$ . Since $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a level- $0$ segment, the values $A_{i}$ and $B_{k-i}$ are constant for all $i\in[i_{0},i_{1}]$ . Because $i\in[i_{0},i_{1}]$ , we have

$$ A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i_{0}}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i_{0}}=A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i}\neq C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k} $$

and

$$ A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}\equiv A_{i}+B_{k-i}\equiv C_{k}\pmod{Q}. $$

Hence, $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is an active level- $0$ segment and thus belongs to $S_{0}$ .

Moreover, the above identities hold for every $i\in[i_{0},i_{1}]$ . For a fixed $k$ , the level- $0$ segments form disjoint maximal intervals, so exactly $i_{1}-i_{0}+1$ indices $i\in[n]$ in this segment satisfy these conditions. Therefore, it is correct that the algorithm increments $s^{\prime}_{k}$ by exactly $(i_{1}-i_{0}+1)$ .

For the running time, Fact 6.7 implies that the number of level- ${\ell_{\max}}$ segments is $\mathcal{O}(n^{1+\mu}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}})$ . Thus, computing $S_{{\ell_{\max}}}$ takes $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/2^{{\ell_{\max}}})=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/M)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ time. For the refinement step, by the guarantee on $Q$ , for each $\ell$ we have $|S_{\ell}|=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ , and each segment in $S_{\ell+1}$ generates only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ subsegments. Since there are $\mathcal{O}(\log M)=\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ levels, the total time for this refinement step is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ . Finally, we scan all segments in $S_{0}$ and perform a constant-time test and update for each segment, so Phase 2 takes $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(|S_{0}|)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ time. ∎

### 6.4 Finding a Good Modulus $Q$

We now construct a good modulus $Q$ , that is, an integer $Q$ with $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ such that, for every level $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , the number of active level- $\ell$ segments is at most $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q)$ . The idea is essentially the same as in Section 4.4.

Let $4\leq R\leq n^{o(1)}$ be a parameter to be fixed later, and let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of primes in $[R/2,R]$ . We take $Q$ to be a product of primes $p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{T}$ , where $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ for all $1\leq t\leq T$ . We choose these primes inductively: at step $t\geq 1$ , we select a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ and multiply it into the current modulus $Q_{t-1}$ , obtaining

$$ Q_{t}:=\prod_{i=1}^{t}p_{i},\qquad\text{where }Q_{0}:=1. $$

For the analysis, it is convenient to track the following quantities:

- 1. Let $X_{\ell,t}$ denote the number of pairs $(([i_{0},i_{1}],k),s)$ , where $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ such that

$$ A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t}}\quad\text{and}\quad A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\neq s. $$

- 2. Let $Y_{\ell,t}$ denote the number of pairs $(([i_{0},i_{1}],k),s)$ , where $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ , such that

$$ A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t}}. $$

Our inductive invariant is that

$$ X_{\ell,t}=n^{1+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{t}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Later, we will choose $R$ so that $X_{\ell,T}=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu}/Q_{T})$ . By the following lemma, $Q_{T}$ is then a good modulus.

#### Lemma 6.13.

For every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , we have $|S_{\ell}(Q_{T})|\leq X_{\ell,T}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ be an active level- $\ell$ segment with respect to $Q_{T}$ . By Definition 6.6, there exists $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ such that $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{T}}$ and $A^{\mathrm{high}}_{i_{0}}+B^{\mathrm{high}}_{k-i_{0}}-C^{\mathrm{high}}_{k}\neq 0$ . We have $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\neq s$ . Indeed $|A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}|\geq 7M/10$ by Fact 6.2, while $|s|\leq 4\cdot 2^{{\ell_{\max}}}<4M/10$ . Thus, each active segment contributes to $X_{\ell,T}$ , and therefore $|S_{\ell}(Q_{T})|\leq X_{\ell,T}$ . ∎

We now choose $p_{t}$ so that the invariant Eq. 5 continues to hold. The base case $t=0$ holds for $Q_{0}:=1$ by Fact 6.7. Now assume Eq. 5 holds for $t-1$ and that $Q_{t-1}$ has been fixed. For any prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , let $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ (resp., $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ ) denote the value of $X_{\ell,t}$ (resp., $Y_{\ell,t}$ ) when $Q_{t}:=Q_{t-1}\cdot p$ . Our goal is to find a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that Eq. 5 holds at step $t$ . Applying the following lemmas inductively yields the existence of the entire sequence $p_{1},\ldots,p_{T}$ .

#### Lemma 6.14.

There exists $p^{*}\in\mathcal{P}$ such that

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p^{*})=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

Moreover, for every $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ , if $p$ is chosen uniformly at random from $\mathcal{P}$ , then

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}\!\bigl[X_{\ell,t}(p)\bigr]=X_{\ell,t-1}\cdot\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log n}{R}\right). $$

#### Proof sketch.

The proof is almost identical to that of Lemma 4.18. For completeness, we briefly indicate the changes.

Fix a level $\ell$ . Let $\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}$ be the set of pairs $(([i_{0},i_{1}],k),s)$ counted by $X_{\ell,t-1}$ , that is, those satisfying

$$ A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q_{t-1}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\neq s, $$

where $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a level- $\ell$ segment and $s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]$ . For a prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , such a pair is counted in $X_{\ell,t}(p)$ if and only if, additionally, $p$ divides $\Delta:=A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}-s$ . Thus,

$$ X_{\ell,t}(p)=\sum_{(([i_{0},i_{1}],k),s)\in\mathcal{X}_{\ell,t-1}}\mathbf{1}\left[p\mid\bigl(A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}-s\bigr)\right]. $$

The remainder of the argument—bounding $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p\sim\mathcal{P}}[p\mid\Delta]$ , taking expectations, and applying Markov’s inequality with a union bound over $\ell\in\{0,\ldots,{\ell_{\max}}\}$ —is identical to that in Lemma 4.18, yielding a prime $p^{*}\in\mathcal{P}$ that satisfies Eq. 6 and the claimed expectation. ∎

#### Lemma 6.15 (Computing $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ ).

We can compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all primes $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all levels $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n)$ time.

#### Proof.

Fix a prime $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and a level $\ell$ , and let $Q^{\prime}:=Q_{t-1}\cdot p$ . We give an algorithm to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for modulus $Q^{\prime}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}n)$ time. Since ${\ell_{\max}}=\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ , $|\mathcal{P}|=\mathcal{O}(R)$ , and $Q^{\prime}\leq Q_{t-1}R$ , the total time over all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and $\ell$ is

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(|\mathcal{P}|\cdot{\ell_{\max}}\cdot Q^{\prime}n\bigr)=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n\bigr). $$

Recall that a level- $\ell$ segment $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ is a maximal interval of valid indices $i$ on which both $\lfloor A_{i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ and $\lfloor B_{k-i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ are constant. Thus, for a fixed $k$ , the segment start indices $i_{0}$ are exactly those valid indices $i\in[\max\{1,k-n\},\min\{n,k-1\}]$ such that either $i=\max\{1,k-n\}$ , or $\lfloor A_{i-1}/2^{\ell}\rfloor\neq\lfloor A_{i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ , or $\lfloor B_{k-i+1}/2^{\ell}\rfloor\neq\lfloor B_{k-i}/2^{\ell}\rfloor$ . More concretely, define a boundary indicator array $I^{A}$ of size $n$ by

$$ I^{A}_{1}:=1,\qquad I^{A}_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\left\lfloor A_{i-1}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\neq\left\lfloor A_{i}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\right]\quad(i\geq 2), $$

and a boundary indicator array $I^{B}$ of size $n$ by

$$ I^{B}_{n}:=1,\qquad I^{B}_{j}:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\left\lfloor B_{j+1}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\neq\left\lfloor B_{j}/2^{\ell}\right\rfloor\right]\quad(j\leq n-1). $$

Then, for a fixed $k$ , the segment start indices $i_{0}$ are exactly those indices $i\in[\max\{1,k-n\},\min\{n,k-1\}]$ such that $I^{A}_{i}=1$ or $I^{B}_{k-i}=1$ . We handle this OR condition by inclusion–exclusion.

Work over the ring $\mathcal{R}:=\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{Q^{\prime}}-1)$ , where $\mathbb{F}$ has characteristic greater than $n$ . Define the following polynomials in $\mathcal{R}[y]$ :

$$ \displaystyle P_{A}^{\mathrm{all}}(x,y) \displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x^{A_{i}\bmod Q^{\prime}}\,y^{i}, \displaystyle P_{A}^{\mathrm{bdry}}(x,y) \displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}I^{A}_{i}\,x^{A_{i}\bmod Q^{\prime}}\,y^{i}, \displaystyle P_{B}^{\mathrm{all}}(x,y) \displaystyle:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x^{B_{j}\bmod Q^{\prime}}\,y^{j}, \displaystyle P_{B}^{\mathrm{bdry}}(x,y) \displaystyle:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}I^{B}_{j}\,x^{B_{j}\bmod Q^{\prime}}\,y^{j}. $$

Compute the three products in $\mathcal{R}[y]$ :

$$ P^{A}:=P_{A}^{\mathrm{bdry}}\cdot P_{B}^{\mathrm{all}},\qquad P^{B}:=P_{A}^{\mathrm{all}}\cdot P_{B}^{\mathrm{bdry}},\qquad P^{AB}:=P_{A}^{\mathrm{bdry}}\cdot P_{B}^{\mathrm{bdry}}. $$

For any $k\in[2,2n]$ and $r\in\{0,\ldots,Q^{\prime}-1\}$ , let $U_{k}(r)$ be the coefficient of $x^{r}y^{k}$ in the polynomial $P^{A}+P^{B}-P^{AB}$ . Then $U_{k}(r)$ equals the number of segment start indices $i_{0}\in[n]$ such that $A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}\equiv r\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ and either $I^{A}_{i_{0}}=1$ or $I^{B}_{k-i_{0}}=1$ . Next define

$$ W(r):=\left|\left\{s\in[-4\cdot 2^{\ell},\,4\cdot 2^{\ell}]:\ s\equiv r\pmod{Q^{\prime}}\right\}\right|\qquad\text{for all }r\in\{0,\ldots,Q^{\prime}-1\}. $$

A level- $\ell$ segment $([i_{0},i_{1}],k)$ contributes to $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ if and only if

$$ A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}-C_{k}\equiv s\pmod{Q^{\prime}}. $$

Equivalently, if $r\equiv A_{i_{0}}+B_{k-i_{0}}\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ , then $s\equiv r-C_{k}\pmod{Q^{\prime}}$ . Thus, grouping by $r$ , the contribution of a fixed $k$ is

$$ \sum_{r=0}^{Q^{\prime}-1}U_{k}(r)\cdot W\!\bigl((r-C_{k})\bmod Q^{\prime}\bigr), $$

and therefore

$$ Y_{\ell,t}(p)=\sum_{k=2}^{2n}\ \sum_{r=0}^{Q^{\prime}-1}U_{k}(r)\cdot W\!\bigl((r-C_{k})\bmod Q^{\prime}\bigr). $$

For the running time, each polynomial product takes $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}n)$ time, and we compute only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ such products. Computing $W$ costs $\mathcal{O}(Q^{\prime})$ , and evaluating the double sum costs $\mathcal{O}(Q^{\prime}n)$ . Hence, for fixed $p$ and $\ell$ , the total time is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Q^{\prime}n)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 6.16.

We can find a prime $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ satisfying Eq. 5; that is $X_{\ell,t}(p_{t})=n^{1+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}(\log^{2}n/R)^{t}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n\bigr)$ time.

#### Proof sketch.

We run the algorithm in Lemma 6.15 to compute $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ for all primes $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and all levels $0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}$ . For each $\ell$ , define $Y^{*}_{\ell,t}:=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ , and choose $p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}$ that minimizes

$$ \Phi(p):=\max_{0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}}\bigl\{Y_{\ell,t}(p)-Y^{*}_{\ell,t}\bigr\}. $$

The same argument as in Lemma 4.20 shows that this choice of $p_{t}$ ensures Eq. 5. Moreover, the running time is dominated by computing all values $Y_{\ell,t}(p)$ , which takes $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(R^{2}Q_{t-1}n\bigr)$ time by Lemma 6.15. ∎

It remains to set the parameters so that the above procedure yields a good modulus.

#### Lemma 6.17 (Computing a Good Modulus).

We can compute a good modulus $Q$ in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn)$ time.

#### Proof.

By inductively applying Lemma 6.16 for $T$ steps, we obtain primes $p_{1},\ldots,p_{T}\in\mathcal{P}$ and a modulus $Q_{T}:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}$ such that

$$ X_{\ell,T}=n^{1+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{T}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}. $$

We take $T=\Theta(\log M/\log R)$ and $R=2^{\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}\right)}$ . Then $M\leq Q\leq Mn^{o(1)}$ and

$$ X_{\ell,T}\leq n^{1+\mu}\cdot\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^{2}n}{R}\right)^{T}\leq\frac{n^{1+\mu+o(1)}}{Q_{T}}\qquad\text{for all }0\leq\ell\leq{\ell_{\max}}, $$

by the same argument as in Lemma 4.22. Hence, $Q_{T}$ is a good modulus. ∎

### 6.5 Combining the Results

#### Theorem 6.18.

There is a deterministic algorithm that solves Problem 8 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn+n^{1+\mu}/M)$ .

#### Proof.

We first compute a good modulus $Q$ via Lemma 6.17 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn)$ . We then compute $s_{k}$ for all $k\in[2,2n]$ via Lemma 6.10 in time $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(Qn)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn)$ . Finally, we compute $s^{\prime}_{k}$ for all $k\in[2,2n]$ via Lemma 6.12 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{1+\mu}/Q\right)=\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\left(n^{1+\mu}/M\right)$ . For each $k\in[2,2n]$ , we output Yes if and only if $s_{k}>s^{\prime}_{k}$ and correctness follows from Lemma 6.4. The total running time is $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn+n^{1+\mu}/M)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.3.

By the reductions in Lemma 6.1, it suffices to solve Problem 8 efficiently. By Theorem 6.18, there is a deterministic algorithm that solves Problem 8 in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn+n^{1+\mu}/M)$ . Take $M=\Theta\!\left(n^{\mu/2}\right)$ by setting $d=\mu/2$ . Then, the two terms balance, yielding the claimed time bound $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(n^{\mu/2+1}\right)$ . ∎
