#### Lemma A.1 ([21, Lemma 3.4]).

Let integer parameter $L\geq 1$ . Let $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{hd\times s},B\in\mathbb{Z}^{s\times hd}$ be input matrices with entries in $[-U,U]$ . Partition the indices $i\in\{1,2,\dots,hd\}$ into $h$ contiguous groups each of size $d$ (so that $i$ belongs to the $\lceil i/d\rceil$ -th group).

Suppose $|A_{i,k}-A_{i^{\prime},k}|\leq L$ holds for all $k\in[s]$ and all $i,i^{\prime}$ in the same group, and $|B_{k,j}-B_{k,j^{\prime}}|\leq L$ holds for all $k\in[s]$ and all $j,j^{\prime}$ in the same group.

Then, for any parameter $q\geq 1$ , we can compute the Min-Plus product $A\star B$ by a randomized algorithm in time complexity

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(h^{2}s+qL\cdot\operatorname*{MM}(hd,s,hd)+h^{2}L\cdot\operatorname*{MM}(d,s/q,d)\right)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(U). $$

Now we derandomize Lemma A.1, thereby derandomizing the $+2$ -approximate APSP algorithm of [21] in $O(n^{2.22548})$ time. For convenience, assume without loss of generality that $U\geq hds$ , so that $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(hds)$ can be suppressed by the $U^{o(1)}$ notation.

#### Lemma A.2.

Lemma A.1 can be derandomized with only $U^{o(1)}$ -factor slowdown.

#### Proof.

The only randomized part in the original proof of [21] is to pick a random prime modulus $p\in\Theta(q\log U)$ . Below we describe how to derandomize this step using the standard recipe which finds a good modulus by iteratively deciding its small prime factors [8]. We omit other parts of the original proof that are unrelated to derandomization.

Following the original notations, use the shorthand $\hat{i}=\lceil i/d\rceil\in[h]$ and $\hat{j}=\lceil j/d\rceil\in[h]$ to denote the groups that contain indices $i\in[hd]$ and $j\in[hd]$ respectively. Define matrix $A^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{h\times s}$ by

$$ A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}\coloneqq\left\lfloor\tfrac{1}{L}\min_{(\hat{i}-1)d<i\leq\hat{i}d}A_{i,k}\right\rfloor. $$

Define the matrix $B^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{s\times h}$ analogously. Let $C^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{h\times h}$ be their Min-Plus product $A^{\prime}\star B^{\prime}$ , which can be computed by brute force in time $O(h^{2}s)$ .

For a modulus $p$ , [21] defined a triple $(\hat{i},k,\hat{j})\in[h]\times[s]\times[h]$ to be a false positive (modulo $p$ ) if it does not satisfy

$$ \left\lvert A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}+B^{\prime}_{k,\hat{j}}-C^{\prime}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}\right\rvert<4, $$

but satisfies

$$ A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}+B^{\prime}_{k,\hat{j}}-C^{\prime}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}\in\{-3,\dots,3\}\pmod{p}. $$

We say a modulus $p$ is successful for $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in[h]\times[h]$ if

$$ |F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p)}|\coloneqq\Big\lvert\Big\{k\in[s]:(\hat{i},k,\hat{j})\text{ is a false positive modulo $p$}\Big\}\Big\rvert\leq\frac{s}{q}. $$

One can compute $|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p)}|$ for all $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in[h]\times[h]$ in $O(h^{2}s)$ total time by brute force.

[21] relied on the fact that, for fixed $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in[h]\times[h]$ , a random prime $p\in\Theta(q\log U)$ is successful with $\geq 0.99$ success probability. Therefore, [21] chose a random sequence of $O(\log h)$ many such moduli which can (with high probability) make every pair $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in[h]\times[h]$ successful at least once.

We shall now deterministically choose $U^{o(1)}$ many moduli $m_{1},m_{2},\dots,m_{U^{o(1)}}\in O(q\cdot U^{o(1)})$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(h^{2}s\cdot U^{o(1)})$ time to make every pair $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in[h]\times[h]$ successful at least once. This would be sufficient for derandomizing the lemma (with $U^{o(1)}$ -factor slowdown compared to the original time bound).

Initialize $P\coloneqq[h]\times[h]$ , which denote the set of pairs for which no moduli have been successful yet. We repeat the following procedure $U^{o(1)}$ times, each time finding a modulus $m$ that makes at least $1/U^{o(1)}$ fraction of pairs in $P$ successful (and removing them from $P$ ):

- • Let $M=\exp({\sqrt{\log U}})$ . Initialize $Q_{0}\coloneqq P$ . Perform the following step for $I\coloneqq\lceil\log_{M}q\rceil$ iterations: In the $i$ -th iteration, – Find a prime (by brute-force enumeration) $p_{i}\in[CM\log U,2CM\log U]$ (where $C>1$ is a sufficiently large absolute constant) such that the set

$$ Q_{i}\coloneqq\big\{(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in Q_{i-1}:|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i})}|\leq\frac{s}{M^{i}}\big\} $$

(9) has size

$$ |Q_{i}|\geq 0.9|Q_{i-1}|. $$

(10) Checking whether a prime $p_{i}$ is satisfactory can be done by brute force in in $O(h^{2}s)$ time. The existence of such $p_{i}$ can be proved as follows: By definition, we have

$$ F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i})}\subseteq\big\{k\in F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})}:A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}+B^{\prime}_{k,\hat{j}}\in C^{\prime}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}+\{-3,\dots,3\}\pmod{p_{i}}.\big\}. $$

(11) For fixed $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in Q_{i-1}$ and $k\in F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})}$ , we know Eq. 7 must be violated, so $\{A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}+B^{\prime}_{k,\hat{j}}-C^{\prime}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-r\}_{r\in\{-3,\dots,3\}}$ are all non-zero integers bounded by $O(U)$ , and thus together have at most $O(\log_{M}U)$ prime factors larger than $M$ . Since the number of primes in the interval $[CM\log U,2CM\log U]$ is at least $\Omega((M\log U)/\log(M\log U))$ by the prime number theorem, the probability that a random prime $p_{i}$ from this interval divides any of $\{A^{\prime}_{\hat{i},k}+B^{\prime}_{k,\hat{j}}-C^{\prime}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}-r\}_{r\in\{-3,\dots,3\}}$ is at most $\frac{1}{10M}$ (for large enough constant $C$ ). Consequently, by Eq. 11 and linearity of expectation,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p_{i}}[|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i})}|]\leq\tfrac{1}{10M}|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})}|. $$

By Markov’s inequality,

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{p_{i}}\Big[|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i})}|\leq\tfrac{1}{M}|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})}|\Big]\geq 0.9. $$

Recall that $|F_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}^{(p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})}|\leq\frac{s}{M^{i-1}}$ for every $(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in Q_{i-1}$ . Hence, by Eq. 9 and linearity of expectation, we have

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{p_{i}}[|Q_{i}|]\geq 0.9|Q_{i-1}|. $$

In particular, there exists a prime $p_{i}$ such that $|Q_{i}|\geq 0.9|Q_{i-1}|$ as claimed. After $I=\lceil\log M_{q}\rceil$ iterations, we have found primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{I}$ . Define modulus $m=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{I}$ . By Eq. 10 (recalling $Q_{0}=P$ ) we have

$$ \big\lvert\big\{(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in P:|F^{(m)}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}|\leq\frac{s}{M^{I}}\big\}\big\rvert\geq|Q_{I}|\geq|P|\cdot 0.9^{I}. $$

Note that $0.9^{I}=0.9^{\lceil\log_{M}q\rceil}\geq 0.9\cdot 0.9^{\log q/\log M}=0.9\cdot 0.9^{\log q/\sqrt{\log U}}\geq 0.9\cdot 0.9^{\sqrt{\log U}}\geq 1/U^{o(1)}$ . Note that $M^{I}=M^{\lceil\log_{M}q\rceil}\geq q$ . So

$$ \big\lvert\big\{(\hat{i},\hat{j})\in P:|F^{(m)}_{\hat{i},\hat{j}}|\leq\frac{s}{q}\big\}\big\rvert\geq|Q_{I}|\geq|P|/U^{o(1)}, $$

that is, the modulus $m$ makes at least $1/U^{o(1)}$ fraction of the pairs in $P$ successful, as wanted. Note that the modulus $m\leq(2CM\log U)^{I}\leq(2CM\log U)^{1+\log_{M}q}=qM\cdot(2C\log U)^{1+\log_{M}q}\leq qM\cdot(2C\log U)^{1+\sqrt{\log U}}\leq q\cdot U^{o(1)}$ as required.

The total time complexity of deterministically finding the moduli is obviously $O(h^{2}s\cdot U^{o(1)})$ . ∎
